articleSummary: Ronald Ross, English physician born May 13, 1857 in Almora, British India, proved malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes, Anopheles, announcing this in 1897 after contracting malaria. He later led Liverpool’s tropical-diseases work and, from 1912 to 1917, directed King’s College Hospital’s Tropical Diseases wing in London while teaching tropical hygiene at Liverpool. He served as a medical adviser to the War Office during World War I and to the Pensions Ministry after the war. From 1926 until his death in 1932, he headed the Ronald Ross Institute and Hospital for Tropical Diseases. His malaria research covered Greece, Cyprus, the Suez region, and West Africa; he authored Malaria Prevention. He died in London on September 16, 1932; streets in India honor him.

articleHeadline: Is Applying A Small Drop Of Citronella Oil Effective Against Dengue?
articleSummary: Seasonal dengue surges in India during the monsoon, driven by Aedes aegypti, are not halted by a single drop of citronella oil. Citronella can repel mosquitoes, but a lone drop provides a tiny, short-lived barrier that evaporates within minutes, leaving most of the body exposed; reapplication every 30–60 minutes is often required. Field conditions—heat, wind, and sweat—undermine lab knockdown efficacy, making citronella a limited, transient protection. Compared with DEET, picaridin, or oil of lemon eucalyptus, it should not be relied upon to prevent dengue. A multi-layer defense is advised: apply EPA/WHO-approved repellents on exposed skin during peak Aedes activity (early morning, late afternoon); wear light, protective clothing; eliminate stagnant water; install barrier nets and screens. Safety note: undiluted citronella can cause skin irritation; dilution is essential.

articleHeadline: Effectiveness of the oral rotavirus vaccine ROTASIIL among children hospitalized with acute gastroenteritis in India
articleSummary: ROTASIIL, a pentavalent oral rotavirus vaccine licensed in 2017 and introduced into India's Universal Immunization Program in 2018, was evaluated for effectiveness against rotavirus gastroenteritis (RVGE) in hospitalized children. Across 32 hospitals in seven states, two multi-center studies (July 2019–December 2023) used a test-negative case-control design to estimate adjusted VE (aVE) for three-dose ROTASIIL. Among 2,243 children aged 3–23 months with acute gastroenteritis, 638 were ELISA-positive for RVGE. Completed three-dose series yielded an aVE against hospitalization due to RVGE of 52% (95% CI 32–66), with a peak of 88% (53–97) in ages 3–5 months. aVE against moderate RVGE was 56% (11–79); against severe RVGE, 54% (31–70). Genotype-specific aVE peaked at 62% (29–80) for G1P[8]. For at least one dose, aVE was 45% (26–60) in 1–23 months. Timely vaccination reduces RVGE hospitalizations, especially in younger children.

articleHeadline: Embrapa develops a simpler and cheaper method to detect tuberculosis
articleSummary: Brazil's Embrapa, in partnership with UFJF and Fhemig, developed RRTB, a cheaper TB diagnostic method that replaces centrifugation with swab-based decontamination and a neutralizing solution (citric acid, ammonium citrate, and sodium citrate).
